PMGT1865 Week 02

PMGT1865 Week 02 — Work Breakdown Structure, Network Planning and CPM

From Scope to a Schedule

A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) is a hierarchical decomposition of the project's scope into deliverables and smaller components. A work package is a lowest-level component that can be estimated, assigned and monitored. Work packages describe the work to be delivered; schedule activities describe the actions needed to deliver it.

A practical scheduling process is:

Define the scope and decompose it into work packages and activities.

Identify the logical dependencies between activities.

Estimate activity durations using the available information and resource assumptions.

Calculate the network's timing, project duration and scheduling flexibility.

Present the schedule, check its resource feasibility and maintain it as conditions change.

An activity dependency specifies how one activity constrains another. A predecessor comes before an activity in the relevant logical relationship; a successor is constrained by it. In a finish-to-start relationship with no lag, a successor cannot start until its predecessor finishes.

Schedule Representations

• A precedence network represents activities and their logical relationships. In an activity-on-node network, each node represents an activity and arrows show dependencies.

• A Gantt chart represents activities as horizontal bars on a time axis. It communicates start times, finish times, durations and overlaps.

• An activity table records durations, predecessors and calculated timing values. It supports both network calculations and the construction of a Gantt chart.

Duration estimates may use comparable previous work, productivity rates, detailed work-package estimates or expert judgement. Estimates should state their units and assumptions. A logical network alone does not establish that sufficient people or equipment are available.

Critical Path Method

The Critical Path Method (CPM) calculates the earliest and latest permissible activity times in a dependency network. For a network with fixed durations, finish-to-start relationships and no lag, the longest start-to-finish path determines the earliest project completion time.

Symbol or term

Definition

d

Activity duration, in the same time units as all schedule values

ES

Early start: earliest feasible activity start

EF

Early finish: earliest feasible activity finish

LS

Late start: latest start that preserves the calculated project finish

LF

Late finish: latest finish that preserves the calculated project finish

Total float

Time an activity can be delayed without delaying project completion, subject to the network logic

Critical path

A continuous start-to-finish path with no total float under the calculated schedule

Use a time-zero convention: an activity starting at time 0 with duration 4 finishes at time 4. All values below are working days.

Forward Pass

Process activities from the start towards the finish:

• An unconstrained starting activity has ES = 0.

• ES = max(EF of all immediate predecessors).

• EF = ES + d.

• The project duration is the largest EF among terminal activities.

The maximum is required because every predecessor must be complete before a finish-to-start successor can begin.

Backward Pass

Process activities from the finish towards the start:

• Set the LF of each terminal activity to the project finish time.

• LF = min(LS of all immediate successors).

• LS = LF − d.

The minimum preserves every successor's latest allowable start.

Total Float and Interpretation

Total float = LS − ES = LF − EF.

Activities with zero total float form the critical path or paths. A delay to a critical activity delays project completion unless another change compensates for it. Positive total float is shared schedule flexibility, not permission to ignore dependencies.
